days.title: Moscow braces for the blow
days.imageCredit: Red Army troops on Red Square, 7 November 1941. Frame from the Soviet film Moscow Strikes Back (1942), public domain.
days.post:
Hundreds of thousands of Muscovites, most of them women, were digging antitank ditches around their city when the panzers started moving again.

On 15 November 1941 the frost had hardened the ground, and Army Group Centre renewed its drive on Moscow. The German Ninth Army struck first, south of Kalinin, and the next day two panzer groups swung north of the capital toward Klin.

Zhukov's Western Front had been sent about 100,000 men, 300 tanks and 2,000 guns, and workers had formed 12 militia divisions. Yet a counterattack Stalin insisted on, against Zhukov's advice, ran straight into the German attack and collapsed.

Was Moscow saved by its generals, or by the people who dug and the deep cold that stopped the panzers?
replies: On 19 November Stalin asked Zhukov: "Are you sure we will be able to hold Moscow? It hurts me to ask you that. Answer me truthfully as a communist." Zhukov said Moscow would be held, but that he needed reserves. By 28 November German tanks were across the Moscow Volga Canal at Yakhroma, and another spearhead was near Krasnaya Polyana, less than 20 miles from the Kremlin. Zhukov's fresh reserve armies held, and in early December the Red Army struck back.

Photos: Red Army troops on Red Square, 7 November 1941. Frame from the Soviet film Moscow Strikes Back (1942), public domain. On the card: Moscow workers beside a newly built armored train, December 1941. Frame from the Soviet documentary In Defense of Native Moscow, Central Studio for Documentary Film, public domain.

Sources: Battle of Moscow, Wikipedia; Ziemke and Bauer, Moscow to Stalingrad, US Army Center of Military History; Jonathan Dimbleby, HistoryNet; State Defence Committee decree of 19 October 1941; Moscow Strikes Back film still, Wikimedia Commons.
days.alt: Archival film still of a line of Red Army soldiers in fur hats and greatcoats, bayonets fixed on their rifles, cheering as they stand in ranks.
facts: 15 November 1941: Army Group Centre renews Operation Typhoon after frost hardens the ground.
German Ninth Army strikes first, south of Kalinin; 3rd and 4th Panzer Groups join on 16 November, aiming at Klin and Solnechnogorsk.
Guderian's Second Panzer Army attacks below Tula on 18 November.
Zhukov's Western Front got about 100,000 men, 300 tanks and 2,000 guns in early November; 12 militia divisions formed.
250,000 to 600,000 Muscovites, most of them women, dug antitank ditches and trenches.
Stalin held the 7 November parade on Red Square; troops marched straight on to the front.
Klin fell 23 November; by 28 November Germans were less than 20 miles from the Kremlin.
Red Army struck back in early December.

days.title: Operation Queen
days.imageCredit: A crewman loads a 4.5 inch rocket into a T27 launcher of the 18th Field Artillery at Mausbach, Germany, 16 November 1944. Frame from U.S. Army Signal Corps film 111-ADC-2715, National Archives, public domain.
days.post:
About 1,200 American heavy bombers hit the German line on 16 November 1944. Prisoners from one German division later put their losses at 1 to 3 percent.

Operation Queen was, by the US Army's own count, the largest air attack of the war in direct support of ground troops. The bombers carried fragmentation bombs, picked to hit men without cratering the roads the Americans would need, while RAF Bomber Command struck Duren, Julich and Heinsberg behind the front. Then 1,246 American guns joined in, and at 12:45 the First and Ninth Armies attacked toward the Roer.

Most forward German positions survived. The telephone lines did not.

Was Operation Queen a waste of the biggest air support ever flown, or did it do enough?
replies: Bad luck struck the German 47th Volks Grenadier Division, which was arriving by train in the Roer towns as the bombs fell. An artillery battalion caught at the Julich railroad station was all but wiped out. On the ground the fight was brutal: by 17 November the rifle companies of the 16th Infantry's 1st Battalion, which had started with about 160 men each, were down to 60 or 70 men, and one to 100.

Photos: A crewman loads a 4.5 inch rocket into a T27 launcher of the 18th Field Artillery at Mausbach, Germany, 16 November 1944. Frame from U.S. Army Signal Corps film 111-ADC-2715, National Archives, public domain. On the card: Ninth Air Force B-26 Marauders over German positions near Eschweiler, Germany, 16 November 1944. NARA 342-FH-3A21246-55093AC, public domain.

Sources: MacDonald, The Siegfried Line Campaign, US Army Center of Military History; Operation Queen, Wikipedia; National Archives photo 342-FH-3A21246-55093AC; Signal Corps film 111-ADC-2715, National Archives.
days.alt: Archival film still of an American soldier in a helmet bending over a frame of rocket launcher tubes, sliding a long rocket into one of them.
facts: 16 November 1944: Operation Queen, the largest air attack of the war in direct support of ground troops (US Army history).
About 1,200 Eighth Air Force heavy bombers dropped 4,120 tons of fragmentation bombs around Eschweiler, Weisweiler and Langerwehe.
RAF Bomber Command hit Duren, Julich and Heinsberg behind the front.
Bomb line kept two miles in front of US troops; one American killed by stray bombs.
1,246 US guns fired; 694 on the First Army front fired an hour long preparation.
Infantry attacked at 12:45 toward the Roer.
German prisoners from one division put losses at 1 to 3 percent, but phone lines were cut.
An artillery battalion of the 47th Volks Grenadier Division was all but wiped out at Julich station.

days.title: The 442nd leaves the Vosges
days.imageCredit: A squad leader of Company F, 442nd Regimental Combat Team, watches for German movement near St Die, France, 13 November 1944. NARA 111-SC-340950, public domain.
days.post:
By 8 November 1944, Company I of the 442nd had no officers left. It was commanded by T/5 Clarence Taba, a corporal promoted on the spot. Company K had 17 riflemen, led by a sergeant.

On 17 November the Army's Japanese American regiment pulled back to Docelles, released from the 36th Infantry Division after more than a month in the Vosges Mountains. In October it had freed Bruyeres, taken Biffontaine and fought through the forest to reach the 211 survivors of the Lost Battalion. The regiment's journal counts 140 killed and 1,800 other casualties in the Vosges.

Was rescuing the Lost Battalion worth what it cost the 442nd?
replies: At Docelles the men finally got hot showers, and 382 new Japanese American replacements joined the regiment. On 19 November the combat team left the Vosges by truck, and three days and 540 miles later it reached St Jeannet near Nice to hold the French and Italian border. The men called it the Champagne Campaign. It was quieter than the Vosges, but shelling, mines and patrols still took lives.

Photos: A squad leader of Company F, 442nd Regimental Combat Team, watches for German movement near St Die, France, 13 November 1944. NARA 111-SC-340950, public domain. On the card: Color guards of the 442nd Combat Team stand at attention as citations are read, France, 12 November 1944. NARA 111-SC-196716-S, public domain.

Sources: Excerpts from the 442nd Journals, 100th Infantry Battalion Veterans Education Center; The Rescue of the Lost Battalion and the Maritime Alps, 100th Infantry Battalion Veterans Education Center; Sons and Daughters of the 442nd RCT; L. Stuart Hirai, History.com; National Museum of the United States Army; National Archives.
days.alt: Archival photo of a helmeted soldier in a field jacket kneeling among snowy pine trees, holding a carbine and looking off to the right.
facts: 17 November 1944: the 442nd pulls back to Docelles, released from the 36th Division after more than a month in the Vosges.
October: freed Bruyeres, took Biffontaine, rescued the 211 survivors of the Lost Battalion (26 to 30 October).
Regimental journal: 140 killed and 1,800 other casualties in the Vosges.
8 November: Company I had no officers, led by T/5 Clarence Taba; Company K had 17 riflemen.
12 November: Dahlquist asked why the whole regiment was not there; told this was all that was left.
382 replacements joined at Docelles.
Left by truck 19 November; 540 miles to St Jeannet near Nice, the Champagne Campaign.

days.title: Patton's men break into Metz
days.imageCredit: German defenders of Metz gathered in a courtyard before being marched to the rear, November 1944. US Army Air Forces photo, NARA 342-FH-3A17755, public domain.
days.post:
Metz was an old fortress city ringed by forts. When the Americans broke in, most of the Germans outside those forts fired a few shots and then walked into the American lines with their hands up.

On 18 November 1944 men of the 5th Infantry Division crossed the city limits from the south while the 95th pressed in from the north and west, and P-47s dive bombed the city. The German army in the field had pulled back east and left the garrison to its fate. Fighting in the city formally ended on 22 November.

The outer forts held out. General Walton Walker forbade assaults on them to save shells and left them to starve. The last, Fort Jeanne d'Arc, held until 13 December.

Was starving the forts the smart call, or did it just drag Metz out?
replies: Early on 18 November the Germans blew the bridges over the Moselle west of the city. One went up while a patrol of the 378th Infantry was crossing it: eight men on the bridge were killed, and five who had already crossed were cut off, though they were later rescued. French resistance fighters of the FFI helped the Americans, and for France the liberation of Metz ended four years of German annexation.

Photos: German defenders of Metz gathered in a courtyard before being marched to the rear, November 1944. US Army Air Forces photo, NARA 342-FH-3A17755, public domain. On the card: German prisoners march through the streets of Metz, France, November 1944. US Army Air Forces photo, NARA 342-FH-3A17756, public domain.

Sources: Hugh M. Cole, The Lorraine Campaign, US Army Center of Military History; Battle of Metz, Wikipedia; Signal Corps film 111-ADC-2717, National Archives; Ville de Metz; Time, 27 November 1944; National Archives photo 342-FH-3A17755.
days.alt: Archival photo of a crowd of German soldiers in greatcoats and caps standing and sitting in a cobbled courtyard beside a truck and low buildings.
facts: 18 November 1944: 5th Infantry Division crosses the Metz city limits from the south; 95th Division presses from the north and west.
P-47s dive bombed the city that day.
Germans blew the Moselle bridges; eight men of a 378th Infantry patrol killed on one.
19 November: US divisions linked up inside the ring.
Most Germans outside the forts gave up after a few shots; no real house to house battle.
FFI fighters and the Mithridate and Navarre networks helped.
Fighting in the city ended 22 November; last fort, Jeanne d'Arc, surrendered 13 December.
German losses in the city: about 400 dead and 2,200 wounded.

days.title: Operation Uranus begins
days.imageCredit: Soviet infantry charge across the snow. Frame from Soviet newsreel footage in The Battle of Russia (1943, U.S. War Department), National Archives 111-OF-5, public domain.
days.post:
When the ring closed at Stalingrad, Soviet commanders believed they had caught 85,000 to 90,000 Axis troops. Estimates of the real number run from about 250,000 to 300,000.

It began on 19 November 1942. After a barrage from about 3,500 guns and mortars, Soviet armies attacked the Romanian Third Army on the Don northwest of the city. The Romanians had no antitank guns heavier than 47 mm, and their line broke by noon. Soviet tank corps drove through the gaps, and on 23 November the two pincers met near Kalach, trapping the German Sixth Army.

Hitler ordered it to hold where it stood and be supplied by air. Was that the decision that lost the war in the east?
replies: The plan was prepared in secret. Between 1 and 19 November, boats of the Volga Flotilla carried 160,000 troops and 430 tanks across the river to the Stalingrad Front, moving at night. At 22:00 on the first day, Army Group B ordered all German attacks inside Stalingrad stopped at once and pulled panzer divisions out of the city. The Sixth Army surrendered at the start of February 1943.

Photos: Soviet infantry charge across the snow. Frame from Soviet newsreel footage in The Battle of Russia (1943, U.S. War Department), National Archives 111-OF-5, public domain. On the card: Soviet tank crews refuel during the winter offensive near Stalingrad, 1942 to 1943. Unknown Soviet photographer, public domain.

Sources: Operation Uranus, Wikipedia; Ziemke and Bauer, Moscow to Stalingrad, US Army Center of Military History; Antony Beevor, Stalingrad; HistoryOfWar.org; The Battle of Russia, National Archives.
days.alt: Archival film still of Soviet infantrymen in greatcoats running across a flat snowy field in a long ragged line under a gray sky.
facts: 19 November 1942: Operation Uranus begins on the Don northwest of Stalingrad.
Code word "Siren" at 07:20 Moscow time; about 3,500 guns and mortars opened fire ten minutes later.
Attack at 08:50 against the Romanian Third Army, whose biggest antitank guns were 47 mm.
Romanian line broke by noon.
Stalingrad Front struck from the south on 20 November.
Pincers met near Sovetsky, east of Kalach, on 23 November.
Trapped: about 250,000 to 300,000; Soviet commanders first thought 85,000 to 90,000.
Sixth Army surrendered at the start of February 1943.

days.title: The Marines land on Tarawa
days.imageCredit: Wrecked amtracs and the log seawall on Betio after the battle, November 1943. National Archives 127-GR-119-63578, public domain.
days.post:
The tide at Betio left only about 3 feet of water over the coral reef. The Higgins boats needed about 4.

On the morning of 20 November 1943 the 2nd Marine Division landed on Betio, the main island of Tarawa Atoll, about 2 miles long and nowhere more than about 10 feet above the sea. The tracked amtracs could crawl over the reef, and within about 10 minutes of the first landing at 9:10 a.m. they had put more than 1,500 Marines ashore. The boats behind them grounded on the reef, and the Marines aboard waded 500 to 1,000 yards to shore under fire.

Organized resistance ended about 76 hours after the first amtrac hit the beach. More than 1,000 Marines and Navy corpsmen were killed.
replies: Of the 125 amtracs used at Betio, only 35 were left at the end. Of the island's defenders, 4,690 died, and only 17 wounded Japanese were taken prisoner, along with 129 Korean laborers. The hard lessons, among them more and better armored amtracs and heavier, more accurate bombardment, shaped every Pacific landing that followed.

Photos: Wrecked amtracs and the log seawall on Betio after the battle, November 1943. National Archives 127-GR-119-63578, public domain. On the card: Marines wade ashore through the shallows off Betio, Tarawa, November 1943. National Archives 32606885, public domain.

Sources: Col. Joseph H. Alexander, Across the Reef, Marine Corps Historical Center; The National WWII Museum; Battle of Tarawa, Wikipedia; National Archives.
days.alt: Archival photo of a shattered log seawall along a beach strewn with debris, wrecked amtracs in the shallows and broken palm trees against the sky.
facts: 20 November 1943: the 2nd Marine Division lands on Betio, Tarawa Atoll (Operation Galvanic).
Betio: about 2 miles long, 800 yards wide, no more than about 10 feet above the sea.
First amtracs ashore at 9:10 a.m.; more than 1,500 Marines landed in about 10 minutes.
Neap tide: about 3 feet over the reef; Higgins boats needed 4; Marines waded 500 to 1,000 yards.
125 amtracs used, 35 left at the end.
Organized resistance ended 1:05 p.m., 23 November, about 76 hours in.
Marine Corps history counts 3,407 casualties; more than 1,000 killed.
4,690 defenders died; 17 Japanese and 129 Korean laborers taken prisoner.

days.title: Jackson opens the case
days.imageCredit: Justice Robert H. Jackson addresses the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg. Photo by Charles Alexander, Office of the US Chief of Counsel, Truman Library 72-874, National Archives, use unrestricted.
days.post:
The man who opened the case against the Nazi leaders at Nuremberg was a sitting justice of the US Supreme Court. Robert H. Jackson took a leave of absence from the Court to do it.

On 21 November 1945, the second day of the trial, Jackson rose before the International Military Tribunal. He said the case would rest on the Nazis' own records: "We will show you their own films. You will see their own conduct and hear their own voices." He told the judges that the real complaining party at their bar was "Civilization", and he finished the whole address that same day.

When the trial ended on 1 October 1946, he went back to his seat on the Court.

Should a sitting Supreme Court justice have taken the job of chief prosecutor?
replies: His most quoted line came early: "The wrongs which we seek to condemn and punish have been so calculated, so malignant, and so devastating, that civilization cannot tolerate their being ignored, because it cannot survive their being repeated." Before he spoke, the defendants entered their pleas. Goering tried to make a statement and was cut off by the presiding judge. Hess simply said "No", which the court entered as not guilty.

Photos: Justice Robert H. Jackson addresses the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg. Photo by Charles Alexander, Office of the US Chief of Counsel, Truman Library 72-874, National Archives, use unrestricted. On the card: Justice Robert H. Jackson presents the prosecution's opening statement at Nuremberg, 21 November 1945. US Army Signal Corps photo, National Archives 111-SC-219750, public domain.

Sources: Nuremberg Trial Proceedings, Avalon Project, Yale Law School; Robert H. Jackson Center; National Archives; David Adler, South Dakota Humanities Council; Nuremberg trials, Wikipedia.
days.alt: Archival photo of the crowded Nuremberg courtroom seen from above, with lawyers at long desks, the defendants in the dock behind them guarded by white helmeted military police, and a wood paneled wall with a clock.
facts: 21 November 1945, second day of the Nuremberg trial: Jackson opens the prosecution's case.
Jackson was a sitting US Supreme Court justice, appointed chief prosecutor by Truman.
Every defendant present pleaded not guilty; Hess just said "No".
Opening line: "The privilege of opening the first trial in history for crimes against the peace of the world imposes a grave responsibility."
"Civilization cannot tolerate their being ignored, because it cannot survive their being repeated."
He called the real complaining party "Civilization" and finished the address that day.
The National Archives holds a recording of the opening in his own voice.
Trial ran to 1 October 1946; Jackson returned to the Court.
